title: Agent guide
body:
# Agent guide

Call `get_guide` on connection and after each learning step. Use the Next Step and the learner’s goal to choose a workflow.

1. **Start together.** Read [how Startodel works](startodel://guide/platform), then [complete the Onboarding Questionnaire](startodel://guide/first-steps). Finish with a first Topic the learner recognizes as relevant.
2. **Plan a Track.** For a technology or comparison, [design and verify a Track](startodel://guide/build-track-technology). For a codebase, [pin the repository revision](startodel://guide/build-track-from-repo) first. Finish with a sourced Track Graph that leads to an agreed task or decision.
3. **Teach and assess.** [Choose the next Topic](startodel://guide/agent-workflow), [write a Lesson](startodel://guide/lessons-and-blocks) when needed, and [work through it with the learner](startodel://guide/user-workflow). For an oral or written assessment, [continue a GrillSession](startodel://guide/grill-session). For due Topics, [conduct a Review](startodel://guide/review-loop). Finish with the learner’s recorded evidence.

Call `resources/list` to discover guide sections and worked examples. Fetch a linked resource with `resources/read` using its `startodel://guide/…` URI.

Tool responses include JSON text and a `structuredContent` object. For a list, read `structuredContent.items`. Share the entity’s `url` with its learner. Read it from `topic.url` on `get_topic` and `session.url` on `start_grill`. On `get_track` and `list_tracks`, a Track published at the Owner’s login also has a `publicUrl` for sharing.

title: How Startodel works
body:
# How Startodel works

Call `get_guide` first. Use the learner’s Profile and goal to choose a Topic, teach its mechanism, then ask the learner to use it. Record their answer and evidence through the Tools. The MCP Token selects the Owner.

1. **Orient.** Read the Next Step and its reason. Use `get_progress` when choosing between studying, a GrillSession and due ReviewItems. Leave the learner with one activity they can start now.
2. **Locate the work.** A Topic lives once in the Owner’s Topic Catalog. Tracks order Topics, and TopicEdges connect prerequisites to dependents. Before teaching, identify the Topic whose Lessons and Mastery will carry across its Tracks.
3. **Close the loop.** Startodel scores Quizzes and schedules Reviews. You assess free-text Exercises and Grill Questions. Finish with the learner’s recorded result and the next action from `get_guide`.

title: Complete the Onboarding Questionnaire
body:
# Complete the Onboarding Questionnaire

On connection, call `get_guide`, then `get_profile`. Use `update_profile` to save the learner’s confirmed Onboarding Questionnaire answers.

1. **Connect.** If the learner needs access, have them issue an MCP Token in Settings and configure their client for Streamable HTTP at the installation’s `/mcp` URL with the Bearer credential in its secret input. Continue when `get_profile` returns the learner’s Profile.
2. **Fill the gaps.** Compare the saved stack, goals and grade with what you already know about the learner. Ask about a current project when it would clarify the goal. Confirm the language for learning content with the learner. Save a confirmed Russian or English UI preference with `update_profile` (`ru` or `en`), or clear it with `null`. Save partial answers as they arrive. Finish when the learner recognizes the stack, goal and grade in your readback.
3. **Agree on a starting point.** Offer a first Topic and an example from their work in their preferred language. Confirm anything uncertain. Mark onboarding complete after the learner confirms the questionnaire, then read `get_guide` for the new Next Step.

title: Working with the learner
body:
# Working with the learner

Use `get_lesson` to teach in chat. After the learner acts, use `mark_lesson_read` for confirmed reading, `record_quiz_result` for their Quiz choices or `set_mastery` for demonstrated depth.

1. **Frame the Lesson.** Name something the learner wants to do in their project. Show a small example, then ask them to predict what it will do. Begin the explanation from the first point where their prediction and the trace diverge, or move to a harder case if they agree.
2. **Hear the reasoning.** Present Quiz prompts and options, then submit the learner’s own choices and discuss the returned feedback. For an Exercise, offer a hint and reveal the solution on explicit request. Finish with the learner’s explanation of what changed in their example.
3. **Record the result.** Capture confirmed reading or actual Quiz choices through the corresponding Tool. Mastery starts at 0. Reading all Lessons in a Topic with at least one Lesson raises it to 1. Fully correct latest Quiz Attempts on all Quizzes in a Topic with at least one Quiz raise it to 2. These automatic rules only raise Mastery. For free-text work, cite the learner’s words or trace. Finish with a saved result and a next Topic or practice task the learner can name.

title: Choose the next Topic
body:
# Choose the next Topic

Use `get_profile`, `get_progress`, `list_tracks` and `get_track_graph` to find a Topic that advances the learner’s goal. Inspect `get_topic` and `list_lessons` before deciding what to teach.

1. **Check readiness.** Choose a Topic below Mastery 2 whose prerequisites have all reached 2, including prerequisites outside this Track. When none qualifies, identify the blocking prerequisite, a cycle or a completed Track before proposing a next move.
2. **Match the learner.** Use their current project or domain to choose an example in the Track’s technology. Adjust depth, pace and prerequisite review to the learner’s experience with this Topic. Keep any foundations they asked to learn. Read an existing Lesson with `get_lesson`, or use the Lesson workflow to write one. Continue when the learner has a specific question they will be able to answer.
3. **Try a variation.** Change one input or constraint and ask the learner to predict the effect. Assess their explanation against the evidence rules, then call `get_guide` once the result is recorded.

title: Design and verify a Track
body:
# Design and verify a Track

Start with `get_profile` and `list_topics` to personalize the plan and find reusable Topics. After research and agreement on the outline, use `create_track`, `upsert_topics`, `add_edges` and `attach_topics_to_track`.

1. **Personalize the outcome.** Combine the Onboarding Questionnaire with what you already know to choose the starting Topic, depth, pace, prerequisites and language. Use examples from the learner’s current project or domain. If they ask to learn from scratch, teach the requested foundations in that technology. Leave out another framework’s code, terminology and side-by-side comparisons unless the learner explicitly asks to compare technologies in this conversation. Confirm the choice if their background or goal is uncertain.
2. **Verify the sources.** Before designing the Track, use your own web and repository tools to verify the current release and read a primary source for each technology. Check official documentation against recent release notes, a maintainer article or the primary repository. Proceed only when each design decision has a supporting source URL and its version or date.
3. **Choose a mode from the goal.** Agree on an outline that ends in an observable decision or working result.
   - **Comparison mode** only when the learner explicitly asks, for example “How do X and Y differ?” Build a mental model of each, including its core problem and architecture. Apply both to the same case. Derive tradeoffs and decision criteria, then vary a constraint. End with a scenario-based Quiz asking which fits the new case, followed by “Why?” in chat.
   - **Deep-dive mode** for “Teach me X.” Connect a mental model to the learner’s concrete goal. Start with a working setup or configuration, trace the internals that explain its behavior, then diagnose a production failure. End with an Exercise where the learner changes the setup and verifies the result independently.
4. **Build and read back.** Reuse matching Topic Slugs. Create the private Track with a one- or two-sentence description of what the learner will be able to do and what the Track covers. Mention a major version briefly if it defines the scope. Set `language` explicitly when you know the language of the content, using a lowercase tag such as `en`, `ru` or `pt-br`. Put versioned documentation and dated release notes in Track Sources. Save the missing Topics, connect prerequisites to dependents and attach members in teaching order. Check `get_track` with either the UUID `id` or the `slug` for the citations and `get_track_graph` for the agreed first Topic and path to the outcome. The Track is ready when both match the plan.
5. **Revise an existing Track.** For a changed content language, source or goal use `update_track`. For an incorrect prerequisite use `remove_edge`. For a Topic that no longer belongs use `detach_topic_from_track`, which preserves its Lessons. Verify the affected sources, edges or memberships on readback.

title: Build a Track from a repository
body:
# Build a Track from a repository

Use `get_profile` to establish the learner’s goal and `list_topics` to find relevant prior work. Ground the Track in a real repository revision before applying the Track design workflow.

1. **Pin the task.** Pair the learner’s project and experience with a change, diagnosis or design choice they want to make. Resolve the target release or branch to a commit. Continue when you can name the task and link to the revision.
2. **Trace one real call.** Use your own repository and web tools to check the release history and official docs against that revision. Follow a public entry point through its implementation to a test that exercises the behavior. Keep a permalink to each and distinguish the public guarantee from the implementation detail. If access is missing, get the source or a verifiable public revision before continuing.
3. **Choose the route.** Use comparison mode only when the learner explicitly asks to compare approaches in this conversation. Trace the same operation on both sides. For a working change, use deep-dive mode. Locate the setup and a failure the learner can reproduce in the repository’s stack. Carry that evidence into **Design and verify a Track**. The outline is ready to build when it names the mode and the pinned revision. Write a one- or two-sentence Track description naming the learner’s task and the part of the repository they will study. Mention the revision briefly if it defines the scope. Put the commit and code permalinks in Track Sources.

title: Write a Lesson with Blocks
body:
# Write a Lesson with Blocks

Use `get_profile` to calibrate the Lesson. Inspect `list_lessons` and `get_lesson` for the Topic, then use `create_lesson` or `update_lesson` once the content meets the criteria below.

1. **Choose a question.** Pick a question from the learner’s project or domain that they can test in the Track’s technology and their preferred language. Choose the depth and number of Blocks the Topic needs. Set no writing target for overall Lesson length or Block count. Before writing the Lesson, use your own web and repository tools to verify the behavior against a current primary source. Record its version or date and the passage, test or implementation that supports the answer.
2. **Show first, explain second.** Open with a minimal runnable or traceable example. Use about 5–10 lines in a `code` Block or a concrete scenario. Show the example before asking for a prediction in a `quiz`. For an unscored reflection, put a short prompt in the `theory` Block that sets up the question. Keep the answer out of the framing, code comments and optional code `explanation`.
3. **Teach one idea per `theory` Block.** Trace the answer step by step in a later `theory` Block. Show what changed and explain why in your own words. A typical explanation takes 60–100 words in one or two short paragraphs. Avoid one-line stubs that just pad the outline. Give each new mechanism its own Block. Alternate explanation with code and quick checks.
4. **Use words the learner can follow.** Explain jargon in plain language on first use. For example, “React can group several state updates together. This is called batching.” If a term needs a later Block or Topic, introduce it there. Write like a colleague at a whiteboard. Use short, direct sentences. Cut academic filler, stock introductions and strings of em dashes.
5. **Make the caveat tangible.** Include a substantive Callout Block (`production`, `gotcha` or `tip`). Reserve it for a tip, gotcha, production caveat or takeaway. Name the non-obvious condition and, where relevant, how to detect or address it. Cut filler Callouts. Never put prediction questions, Quiz prompts or Exercise prompts in a Callout.
6. **Make citations clickable.** Cite the verified primary source in a Link Block or Video Block with its version or date and what to inspect. For an inline citation, label the Markdown link with the publisher and page title. Move background reading to Track Sources. Remove unlinked parenthetical titles.
7. **Test understanding.** Use a Quiz to apply the idea or diagnose a failure, or a transfer Exercise that changes a constraint and asks for a prediction, fix or trace. Give feedback that explains the decisive condition.
8. **Check the saved Lesson.** When replacing Blocks, retain the content and stable IDs the learner still needs. Read the Lesson back with `get_lesson`. Check the order as well as the mechanism, example, substantive Callout, dated or versioned primary citation, and Quiz or Exercise.

## Good vs Bad Lesson opening

**Bad** (`theory`) “As an experienced developer, you’ll recall that primitive assignment, binding reassignment and snapshot semantics explain why the first log prints 2.”

**Good** (`code`)

```js
// Save a player's score, then add a point.
let score = 2;
const before = score;
score += 1;
console.log(before);
console.log(score);
```

- `quiz` “Which two numbers will you see, in order?” Choose “2 then 3” or “3 then 3”.
- `theory` “The first log prints 2. When you saved `before`, `score` held the number 2. Adding a point changed only `score`, so the second log prints 3.”

For the complete [browser tasks Lesson](startodel://guide/references/browser-tasks), call `resources/read` with URI `startodel://guide/references/browser-tasks`. Its Link Block names the standard and points to the exact steps to trace.

## Block checklist

1. Give each Block a `type` and a unique, stable `id` of 1–64 letters, digits, underscores or hyphens. The schema accepts up to 200 ordered Blocks per Lesson.
2. Help learners scan the sticky Lesson contents sidebar. Set a short, descriptive `title` on major Theory, Callout and Exercise Blocks. Use the filename for a Code Block when it fits, for example `timers.cjs`. These titles are optional and accept up to 120 characters. Without one, the sidebar falls back to a short phrase from the body. For code it uses the code explanation, then the first line of code.
3. Give each Link and Video a title naming the resource. A Quiz can take an optional `title` of up to 120 characters, but its sidebar entry always shows the question count and ignores that `title`.

| Type       | Required content                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `theory`   | `markdown`                                                                                                                                                     |
| `code`     | `language` and `code`, optionally `explanation`                                                                                                                |
| `callout`  | `markdown` and `variant` (`gotcha`, `production` or `tip`)                                                                                                     |
| `link`     | `title` and HTTP(S) `url`, optionally `note`                                                                                                                   |
| `video`    | `title` and a YouTube video `url`, optionally `note`                                                                                                           |
| `quiz`     | 1–10 `questions`, each with a `prompt`, 2–6 nonempty `options` and a zero-based `correctIndex` into those options. Each question may include an `explanation`. |
| `exercise` | `prompt` and `solution`, optionally a list of `hints`                                                                                                          |

title: Continue a GrillSession
body:
# Continue a GrillSession

Use `get_profile` to set the level. Resume with `list_grills` and `get_grill`, or open a new GrillSession with `start_grill`. Use `judge_grill_answer` for a stored response, or `submit_grill_answer` when the learner answers in chat.

1. **Choose questions.** Use `get_grill_candidates` to choose due or weak Topics and `add_grill_questions` to save prompts linked to them. At the learner’s level, test recall, application and explanation. Start with a familiar project behavior, change one constraint, then ask why the prediction holds. Finish with an ordered set of prompts the learner can answer individually.
2. **Hear one answer.** Ask one Grill Question and wait. Use `submit_grill_answer` for the learner’s own chat or spoken response. For an answer already submitted in the app, use the text returned by `get_grill`. Continue once the question has a stored answer.
3. **Judge the reasoning.** Quote the part of the answer that determined the Verdict. Use `judge_grill_answer` to save the Verdict, quote and a specific correction or harder follow-up. The question is assessed when its stored answer has a Verdict and feedback, even if the GrillSession has since finished.
4. **Close the round.** Use `finish_grill` and discuss the weakest Topic or next challenge. A partial or weak Verdict already refreshes the linked ReviewItem. Finish with one practice task tied to the learner’s evidence.

title: Review due Topics
body:
# Review due Topics

Use `list_due_reviews` to choose a due ReviewItem and `get_profile` to calibrate practice. For an agent-led Review, record the Verdict with `record_review_result`. Use `set_mastery` for a change in demonstrated depth.

1. **Choose practice.** Read the due Topic and the last reason. For a Topic with Quizzes, offer the in-app Practice Quiz. Submission records Quiz Attempts and reschedules the ReviewItem. That branch ends with the returned result and next due time. For a free-text Review, agree on a task at the learner’s current level.
2. **Retrieve and transfer.** Test recall, application and explanation. Ask for the mental model from memory, then change one condition in a case from their project or domain that uses the Topic’s technology and ask what happens and why. Wait for the learner’s own prediction and reasoning.
3. **Assess once.** Quote the part of the answer that determined the Verdict in the recorded reason. Tie the quoted reasoning to the shared strong, partial or weak criteria. Finish with one recorded ReviewItem update and its next due time.
4. **Choose the next challenge.** Use the shared Mastery criteria for evidence of greater depth. If the learner missed a condition, ask for a corrected prediction in a fresh case. End with a specific follow-up they can try before the next Review.

title: Rules for external agents
body:
# Rules for external agents

Call `get_guide` on connection and after each learning step. Use the returned Next Step and its reason to pick the workflow.

1. **Personalize first.** Use `get_profile` to combine the Onboarding Questionnaire with what you already know about the learner’s stack, experience, current project and preferred language. Choose the starting Topic, depth, pace and prerequisites. Move quickly through prerequisites they can already demonstrate. Draw examples or a concrete analogy from their project or domain, and ask the first question in their preferred language. If uncertain, confirm the choice with the learner.
2. **Teach the requested technology.** If the learner asks to start from scratch, teach its foundations even if they know another framework. Leave out another framework’s code, terminology and side-by-side comparisons unless the learner explicitly asks for a comparison in this conversation. For a React Track, write the project example in React even if the Profile lists Vue. In every Lesson, explain jargon in plain language on first use or introduce it in a later Block.
3. **Size the Lesson to the Topic.** Choose the depth and number of Blocks the Topic needs. Set no writing target for overall Lesson length or Block count. Teach one idea per `theory` Block. Avoid one-line stubs and filler Callouts.
4. **Record evidence.** Use the learner’s own answer. For free text, a strong Verdict means the answer addresses the prompt accurately, partial identifies a sound idea missing a material condition, and weak identifies faulty reasoning or an inability to apply the idea. Set Mastery 3 only with evidence that the learner explains the mechanism, or 4 with a trace of the internals. Save the specific evidence with `set_mastery`.
5. **Protect the Owner.** The MCP Token selects the Owner. Never pass User or Owner IDs to a Tool. Keep credentials out of prompts and learning records. If a token is lost, direct the learner to revoke it in Settings. Before a large rewrite, identify all affected Tracks and get the learner’s agreement. Preserve Topic Slugs and Block IDs across edits.
6. **Publish by request.** Tracks start private. Use `set_track_visibility` only when the learner explicitly requests that visibility change in this conversation. Publishing requires current Terms Acceptance in the app. If missing, direct the learner to the Track to accept the Publishing rules and Terms of Use. A Public Track shares Track Sources, member Topics and Lessons. Its public Lesson preview hides Quiz answers and Exercise solutions. A Fork starts private with working practice. Check the resulting visibility against the request.

title: Browser tasks and timers
